title: AI Is Changing Customer Success But Not Its Mission
summary: AI in customer success is changing roles, tech, and how postsale work gets done, but the mission of helping customers realize value remains.
body_markdown:
I’ve attended four industry events since September, and while the agendas and audiences differed a bit, I kept hearing variations of the same ideas about where customer success (CS) is headed: Context matters more as AI takes on more work; outcomes matter more than activity; postsale roles are changing; and as the barrier to execution falls, human judgment becomes more valuable.


Individually, none of these ideas are particularly surprising, but hearing them repeatedly over a few months got my attention. Then last week, those ideas started showing up in more concrete ways.


Bain published


[The Rebirth of Customer Success](https://www.bain.com/insights/the-rebirth-of-customer-success/) , making the case that the traditional CS model needs to evolve significantly. Gainsight went a step further. Alongside an organizational restructuring, CEO Chuck Ganapathi announced that the company is “refounding” itself around what it calls the “agentic economy,” moving from selling CS software toward delivering retention as an outcome.


Both make big claims about where CS is headed. I don’t agree with all of them. But the overlap between what I heard at these events, the Bain article, and Gainsight’s announcements is hard to ignore. Together, these signals point to something bigger than another round of changes to the customer success manager (CSM) role: AI is forcing companies to rethink how postsale work gets done, not redefining the mission of CS.


Here are four shifts that show what the rethink requires.


### **More AI Requires Better Customer Context**


AI without context can be worse than no AI at all.


Agents can summarize information, recommend actions, and increasingly execute work. But their effectiveness depends on what they know about the customer. And in most companies, that context still lives across CRM, product, support, marketing, CS, finance, and other systems.


That problem gets more consequential as AI does more.


Giving every team another AI tool won’t create a better customer experience if each tool works from a different version of the customer. Companies need to make consistent customer context available across the enterprise so humans and AI can work from the same understanding of the customer’s goals, history, behavior, and progress. This is a data challenge but isn’t just a data challenge; it’s bigger. It changes how teams work together around the customer.


### **Outcomes Over Output**


For years, CS teams have tracked the things they do: calls, business reviews, success plans, onboarding milestones, campaigns, and other activities. Those metrics can tell you whether work happened. They can’t tell you whether that work helped the customer make progress. This distinction was everywhere at the events I attended. And now both Bain, Gainsight, and others are putting outcomes at the center of their arguments.


That direction makes sense, but we need to be precise about what accountability for outcomes actually means.


Retention, expansion, and net revenue retention don’t result from the work of one individual or function. Product, sales, services, marketing, support, CS, and the customer themselves can all influence the outcome. My recent research on


[CS measurement](https://www.forrester.com/report/fix-the-disconnect-between-customer-success-execution-and-results/RES202429) makes this distinction explicit: Business outcomes have cross-functional ownership. Measuring CS requires gathering evidence that its work contributes to customer progress and, ultimately, business results, not simply holding CS responsible for the final number.


AI makes getting this right even more important. If technology lets teams execute dramatically more activity, counting that activity becomes even less meaningful. Don’t automate activity for activity’s sake. Measure what helps customers make progress, and then automate what matters.


### **Postsale Roles Are Changing**


I’ve heard about new roles and titles at nearly every event: outcome-oriented roles, technical roles, strategic account roles, digital roles, AI-enabled roles, and different combinations of responsibilities that once belonged primarily to the CSM.


Bain proposes replacing the CSM generalist model with a “success architect,” supported by specialists and AI agents. Gainsight is introducing its own version, an “outcome executive” supported by forward-deployed engineers and agents. I’m less interested in what we call these jobs than in why companies are creating them.


The traditional assumption that one CSM should own the relationship, coordinate the journey, understand the product, drive adoption, demonstrate value, manage risk, and influence renewal was always a lot to ask of one person. AI gives companies an opportunity to reconsider that design.


The important question isn’t whether the title “customer success manager” survives. It’s what work customers need from their vendors, who or what is best equipped to do that work, and how those resources come together across the customer journey. That requires designing how postsale work comes together around the customer, not simply putting a renamed role at its center. New titles alone won’t change how the work gets done. Changing the division of work without changing how that work comes together simply creates a different set of silos.


### **Human Judgment Matters More, Not Less**


AI lowers the barrier to execution. It can prepare the meeting, summarize the account, draft the outreach, identify the signal, trigger the workflow, and increasingly act on behalf of the team. That doesn’t make people irrelevant. It changes where they create value. As execution becomes easier, judgment becomes more valuable. Someone still needs to decide which signal matters, whether the recommended action makes sense, when the customer’s situation requires an exception, and what the organization should do when the obvious answer isn’t the right one.


And


*relationships still matter* . Customers don’t simply need information from their vendors. At important moments, they need someone who understands their business, can challenge their thinking, navigate ambiguity, and earn their trust.


This is why I struggle with predictions that AI will simply replace customer-facing teams. The more interesting questions are about the types of work that machines should perform and where human expertise, judgment, and relationships can create greater value.


Gainsight’s announcement describes a “human in the loop” approach that pairs agents with human expertise and judgment. That is much closer to what I have been hearing than a future in which autonomous agents simply take over postsale work.


### **Don’t Confuse A Changing Model With A Changing Mission**


Bain writes that the core mission of customer success hasn’t changed, and I agree.


Helping customers realize value from what they buy remains fundamental. Retention and growth still depend on customers making meaningful progress toward what they set out to achieve. What


*is* changing is how companies organize around that mission. That’s the connection I see across four industry events, Bain’s argument, and Gainsight’s restructuring.


AI is changing who and what performs the work. That puts a different burden on leaders: Define the desired postsale outcomes, make customer context available across human and AI resources, and consciously decide where automation, expertise, and relationships each add value.


None of this means that customer success is disappearing — quite the opposite. What it does mean is that we should stop assuming the function, roles, technology, and operating models that got us here are necessarily the ones that will carry us forward.


The mission remains — the model is up for debate.
